observation: A contextually relevant learned Double procedure increased search cost on an easy 3x task.
impasse: Relevance alone does not imply that activating retrieved knowledge is computationally useful.
teacherQuestion: What distinguishes cases where retrieved knowledge helps from cases where it hurts?

hypotheses.reason: Easy 3x: primitive-only explored 5 candidates; retrieved learned-first explored 10.

hypotheses.statement: Activate retrieved knowledge only when expected utility exceeds its overhead.
hypotheses.reason: Hard 8x: primitive-only explored 434 candidates; learned-first explored 82.

experiments.question: Compare primitive-only and retrieved learned-first search on easy and harder tasks.
experiments.expectedDiscrimination: If relevance is sufficient, learned-first should win both; if utility is separate, it may win only some regimes.

conclusion: Retrieval and activation are separate cognitive decisions.

extractedKnowledge.description: Use retrieved knowledge only when expected benefit exceeds activation/search overhead.
A relevant procedure may be deliberately ignored when primitive execution/search is expected to be cheaper.
When a strategy helps in one case and hurts in another, ask what feature distinguishes the regimes and construct discriminating examples.

nextQuestion: How can expected search utility be predicted before paying the cost of running both search arms?
